title: Generative AI Adoption in Postsecondary Education, AI Hype, and ChatGPT’s Launch
venue: Open/Technology in Education, Society, and Scholarship Association Journal
extended_summary:
This paper examines the early public and educational response to ChatGPT’s launch, focusing on how generative AI was framed in mainstream discourse and what those framings meant for postsecondary education. Rather than evaluating a classroom intervention or measuring student outcomes, the paper asks how AI hype influenced educators’ and institutions’ understanding of generative AI during the first six months after release.

The paper uses critical discourse analysis and interpretive reading of two news sources, The Globe and Mail and The Economist, along with related public and organizational texts, to analyze how ChatGPT was represented. The author argues that news and public discourse produced four dominant themes: overwhelming capability, impending job loss, anthropomorphism of AI, and vulnerability/fear/existential risk. These themes shaped how students, teachers, and administrators perceived ChatGPT and contributed to panicked rather than measured adoption.

The context is postsecondary education in Canada and broader international English-language media discourse, with ChatGPT as the focal generative AI tool. The paper concludes that hype can distort adoption practices, delegitimize educators’ expertise, and encourage fear-based responses. It recommends more deliberate, ethically grounded planning for generative AI in education, including attention to digital literacy, co-design, marginalized communities, and responsible policy development.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed article, but it is a critical discourse analysis and commentary on media narratives rather than an empirical evaluation of a learning intervention. It provides no experimental, quasi-experimental, or outcome-measure evidence for educational effects of generative AI use.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper has clear relevance to education policy and teacher-facing generative AI adoption, but it reports no measured impact sizes on learners or teachers. Its impact is mainly conceptual and systemic, not empirically demonstrated.

interventions.use_case: ChatGPT as a generative AI chatbot discussed as an educator- and student-facing tool for drafting lesson plans, generating quiz questions, providing writing feedback, tutoring support, and critiquing AI-generated text in postsecondary education.

finding.finding_summary: This paper does not test learning outcomes; it qualitatively analyzes how news discourse shaped postsecondary adoption of ChatGPT during the first six months after launch. Across 55 education-related news articles, it finds that hype, fear, and uncertainty influenced institutional thinking about policy, governance, and responsible adoption, with four dominant themes: overwhelming capabilities, impending job loss, anthropomorphism, and existential risk.
finding.measure: Critical discourse analysis of 55 education-related news articles (44 Globe and Mail, 11 The Economist) mentioning ChatGPT

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that ChatGPT was publicly framed as highly efficient for educators and students, especially for drafting, brainstorming, generating prose, and speeding up routine academic work. However, this is a discursive/interpretive finding rather than a measured productivity effect, so no effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Qualitative analysis of claims about time-saving, drafting, and automation in mainstream discourse and OpenAI educator examples
finding.study_size: n=55 articles plus OpenAI educator-facing examples
